statement.p: Use the Divergence Theorem to evaluate the surface integral \iint_{\mathcal{S}} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} .
\mathbf{F} = \left\lt 4 x+y, z,4 z-x\right>, \mathcal{S} is the boundary of the region between the paraboloid z=64-x^2-y^2 and the xy-plane.

static.solution:
\mathbf{F} = \left\lt 4 x+y,z,4 z-x \right>, \text{div} (\mathbf{F})=\frac{\partial }{\partial x}(4 x+y)+\frac{\partial }{\partial y}(z)+\frac{\partial }{\partial z}(4 z-x)=4+0+4=8\text{.} With r_0=8
Using the Divergence Theorem we have \iint_{\mathcal{S}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} =\iiint_{\mathcal{W}} \text{div} (\mathbf{F}) \,dV=\iiint_{\mathcal{W}} 8 \,dV We compute the triple integral: \iint_{\mathcal{S}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_{\mathcal{W}} 8 \,dV=\iint_{\mathcal{D}} \int_0^{64- x^2- y^2}8 \,dz \,dx \,dy= \iint_{\mathcal{D}} 8 z\bigg|_0^{64- x^2- y^2} \,dx \,dy=\iint_{\mathcal{D}} 8(64- x^2- y^2) \,dx \,dy With r_0=8
We convert the integral to polar coordinates: x=r\cos\theta, \quad y=r\sin\theta, \quad 0\le r\le 8, \quad 0\le \theta \le 2\pi \iint_{\mathcal{S}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_0^{2\pi } \int_0^{8} 8\left(64-r^2\right)r \,dr \,d\theta =16\pi \int_0^{8}(64 r- r^3) \,dr= 16\pi \left(\frac{64 r^2}{2}-\frac{r^4}{4}\bigg|_0^{8}\right)= 16384 \pi
